nodes.name: Sunlight is a mix
nodes.statement: Sunlight contains every visible wavelength, from violet near 400 nm to red near 700 nm. Together they look white.

nodes.name: Air molecules are tiny
nodes.statement: Nitrogen and oxygen molecules are about 0.3 nm across, more than a thousand times smaller than a wavelength of visible light.

nodes.name: Induced dipole
nodes.statement: The oscillating electric field of a light wave pushes a molecule's electrons back and forth, turning the molecule into a tiny oscillating dipole.

nodes.name: Oscillating dipoles radiate
nodes.statement: An oscillating dipole sends out light at its driving frequency in many directions. This re-emission is what scattering is.

nodes.name: Power grows as ω⁴
nodes.statement: A small oscillating dipole radiates power proportional to ω⁴, the fourth power of its frequency, because the radiated field follows the acceleration of the charges.

nodes.name: Rayleigh's 1/λ⁴ law
nodes.statement: For particles much smaller than the wavelength, the scattered intensity is proportional to 1/λ⁴. This is Rayleigh scattering.

nodes.name: Blue outscatters red
nodes.statement: Blue light at 450 nm is scattered about (700/450)⁴ ≈ 5.9 times more strongly than red light at 700 nm.

nodes.name: Skylight is scattered sunlight
nodes.statement: Light from a patch of sky away from the Sun is sunlight that air molecules have scattered toward the observer.

nodes.name: The sky looks blue
nodes.statement: Short wavelengths dominate the scattered light, so the daytime sky away from the Sun looks blue.

nodes.name: Violet scatters even more
nodes.statement: By the 1/λ⁴ law, violet light near 400 nm is scattered more strongly than blue light.

nodes.name: Sunlight has less violet
nodes.statement: The solar spectrum falls off toward short wavelengths, so sunlight carries noticeably less violet than blue.

nodes.name: Eyes are weak at violet
nodes.statement: Human eyes are much less sensitive to violet than to blue, because all three types of cone cell respond weakly near 400 nm.

nodes.name: Cone signals mix
nodes.statement: Scattered skylight excites the short-wavelength cones strongly and the other two types partly. The brain reads this mix as a pale blue.

nodes.name: Why not violet
nodes.statement: The sky looks blue rather than violet because sunlight holds less violet, eyes are less sensitive to it, and the cone signals combine to a blue hue.

nodes.name: Longer path at sunset
nodes.statement: When the Sun sits on the horizon, its light crosses about 38 times as much air as when the Sun is straight overhead.

nodes.name: Blue is scattered out
nodes.statement: Along a long path through air, most blue light is scattered out of the direct beam, while red and orange light gets through.

nodes.name: Red sunsets
nodes.statement: The setting Sun and the clouds it lights look red and orange, because the light reaching them has lost most of its blue.

nodes.name: Scattering at 90° polarizes
nodes.statement: A dipole cannot radiate along its own axis of oscillation. So light scattered at 90° to the incoming beam is polarized.

nodes.name: Polarized skylight
nodes.statement: Skylight is most strongly polarized in a band 90° from the Sun, reaching about 75% on a clear day.

nodes.name: Polarizers darken the sky
nodes.statement: A polarizing filter turned to block that band makes the blue sky look much darker, which photographers use to boost contrast.

nodes.name: Bees read polarization
nodes.statement: Bees and many other insects can sense the polarization pattern of the sky and use it to find the Sun's direction when the Sun is hidden.

nodes.name: Mie scattering
nodes.statement: Particles about as large as the wavelength or larger, such as cloud droplets around 10 μm across, scatter all visible wavelengths about equally.

nodes.name: Clouds are white
nodes.statement: Clouds look white because their droplets scatter every color about equally, and repeated scattering keeps the colors mixed.

nodes.name: Thick clouds look gray
nodes.statement: Very thick clouds look gray underneath, because most of the light is scattered back out the top before it reaches the base.

nodes.name: Haze whitens the sky
nodes.statement: Dust, smoke and pollution add larger particles that scatter by Mie scattering, so a hazy sky looks paler and whiter than a clean one.

nodes.name: The horizon is paler
nodes.statement: The sky near the horizon looks paler than overhead, because light from there has been scattered many times along its long path, mixing the colors back toward white.

nodes.name: Space has a black sky
nodes.statement: Above the atmosphere there is no air to scatter sunlight, so the sky looks black even when the Sun is up.
